title: The Hour AI Gave Back, and Who Took It
author: The Slow AI
summary: The Slow AI dissects two widely quoted teacher-AI surveys to challenge the headline claim that AI is meaningfully reducing teacher workload, arguing the reported figures answer how a week felt rather than what actually happened to it. A YouGov poll found 80% of UK teachers now use AI regularly and 51% say it reduced their workload, but England's own Department for Education instrument shows directed time, the legally capped hours a headteacher can require, doesn't flex with AI adoption at all, meaning the load inside a fixed number of hours can shrink while the hours themselves stay exactly where they were. The piece's sharpest methodological critique targets the American Gallup/Walton claim that AI saves teachers "six weeks" a year, showing that figure only holds if a teacher's week is 37 hours, and against the roughly 50-hour week English teachers actually report, the same underlying saving becomes four and a half weeks, while three of the four things Gallup found teachers doing with the time (more nuanced feedback, individualized lessons, parent emails) are simply more work, not free time. Invoking C. Northcote Parkinson's 1955 observation that work expands to fill the time available, illustrated with his own Admiralty staffing data showing officials multiplying while ships and sailors declined, the piece proposes a personal fix in place of trusting national survey headlines: a two-week, five-minutes-a-day ledger tracking exactly where each unit of AI-saved time actually went, since no national survey can answer that question for any individual teacher.
points: The piece's central methodological distinction, 51% reporting reduced workload (how the week felt) versus England's DfE directed-time data (what actually happened to the hours), exposes that a felt sense of lighter workload can coexist with literally zero change in the legally capped hours a teacher is required to work.

The unit-conversion critique of the Gallup 'six weeks a year' claim is precise and damning: the figure only holds if a teacher's week is 37 hours, but against the roughly 50-hour week English teachers actually report, the identical underlying time-saving becomes four and a half weeks, nearly a 25% inflation from an unstated denominator.

The piece flags that three of Gallup's own four reported uses of 'saved' time, more nuanced feedback, individualized lessons, and parent emails, are simply additional work product, not leisure or reduced hours, directly undercutting the workload-relief framing the same survey is used to support.

The Parkinson's Law citation is grounded in verifiable historical data, not just a quotable aphorism: between 1914 and 1928 Royal Navy ships in commission fell from 62 to 20 and personnel from 146,000 to 100,000 while Admiralty officials rose from 2,000 to 3,569, giving the essay's warning about saved time being reabsorbed by an organization a concrete historical precedent.
quotes: The hour that AI hands back to you does not belong to you. A YouGov poll of 1,033 UK teachers, published in August, found that around 80% of them now use AI regularly, which is double the figure of a year ago.
The 51% and the 35% occur in the same sentence of the same report and answer questions about two different things. One asks a teacher how the week felt. The other asks what happened to it.
Six weeks only works if a teacher's week is 37 hours. Against the ~50-hour week English teachers report to the DfE, the same saving is four and a half.

In the study's own words, they reinvest it into providing more nuanced student feedback, creating individualized lessons, writing emails to parents and getting home to their families at a more reasonable time. Three of those four are more work. Better work, quite possibly. But they are still work.
It is a commonplace observation that work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.

If AI saved you four hours last term, those four hours are somewhere, and somebody decided where. That happens to released time in any organisation with a budget and a line manager. Teachers are just the group somebody finally counted.
